newsitem.title: UK: MARK MOSTLY FIRMER ON CROSSES, AWAITS BUBA REPO.
newsitem.headline: MARK MOSTLY FIRMER ON CROSSES, AWAITS BUBA REPO.

text.p: The mark was mostly firmer on its European crosses but activity was thin amid speculation the Bundesbank may switch to variable-rate tenders for security repurchase agreements this week, said traders.
"The focus is on tomorrow and the market is nervous. But 70 percent don't expect the Buba to move," said Ernesto Ramirez, European economist at Bankers Trust.
The Bundesbank is scheduled to set its next weekly repo auction on Tuesday and reveal what form the tender will take - fixed rate, variable-rate or a combination.
Ramirez was expecting a fixed and variable repo.

At 0845 GMT mark/French franc was trading at 3.3691/96 against 3.3698/03 in late Europe on Friday. Against the Italian lira, the mark was at 976.30/60 against 974.90/975.70. It was up at 81.75/77 Swiss francs against 81.58/61.

Analysts and traders said the mark had been given a boost after Bundesbank Chief Economist Otmar Issing was quoted in the Boersen-Zeitung newspaper on Friday as saying that German price developments were moving in the wrong direction. The market took this to mean that the mark was too low against the dollar and rates may be hiked to quell inflation. Dollar/mark, however, was firmer on Monday.
Traders said it had recovered after slumping in the U.S. following the Issing comments. At 0900 GMT it was trading at 1.8545/55 against 1.8470/80 in late Europe.

"I think people are going to be more and more worried about the potential developments of interest rates in Germany and when we will see the impact on German inflation," said Audrey Childe-Freeman, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Saturday that foreign exchange markets ultimately follow fundamental and economic data. "These figures are good in Germany and are getting better," he said.
Waigel, in interviews on Sunday, also said German Chancellor Helmut Kohl should replace several ministers before launching the 1988 election campaign.
Waigel said a number of ministers were only trying to hang on to their jobs until the election, and urged Kohl to jettison any who were tiring well before the 1998 campaign starts.
Analysts said they would keep an eye on developments, but an imminent reshuffle seemed unlikely.
"I don't think there will be anything major, in terms of a political crisis," said Bankers' Ramirez.
